extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in mathematics (complex analysis, asymptotics, analytic number theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Appendix material giving rigorous conditions and techniques for asymptotic evaluation (steepest descent, Laplace's method, generating-function singularity analysis, Hardy–Ramanujan partition asymptotics) and topological/complex-analytic statements and proofs around simple connectivity and the Jordan curve theorem. Targeted at readers learning to apply these methods and theorems carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steepest descent method conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) Im(F) = 0 on Γ. (b) Re(F) has a minimum on Γ at some point z0, and this function is non-degenerate in the sense that the second derivative of Re(F) along Γ is strictly positive at z0. Conditions (a) and (b) imply of course that F'(z0) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If F''(z0) ≠ 0 then two orthogonal curves Γ1 and Γ2 pass through z0 on which F is real; choose the branch (Γ1) where Re(F) has a minimum (steepest descent path) and reject the branch giving a maximum. This justifies deforming the original contour to Γ1 and applying Laplace-type asymptotics near z0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contour deformation via Cauchy theorem requires arc decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Justify replacement of a real-axis integral by an integral on Γ by applying Cauchy's theorem to e^{−sF(z)} on a contour Γ_R made of segments of the real axis, Γ inside a circle of radius R, and the two arcs joining them; contributions of the arcs must tend to zero as R → ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify exponential decay of e^{−sF(z)} on the joining arcs (e.g., e^{−sF(z)} = O(e^{−c y x^2}) or similar) so that arc integrals are O(1/R) or o(1). This is a necessary analytic hypothesis for contour deformation to be legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's method / Proposition 2.1 applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply Laplace's method one needs a real-valued phase Φ with a non-degenerate minimum at an interior point θ0 (Φ(θ0) minimal and Φ''(θ0) > 0) and an amplitude ψ with ψ(θ0) ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under these hypotheses the main contribution to ∫ e^{-sΦ(θ)} ψ(θ) dθ as s→∞ is (ψ(θ0) e^{-sΦ(θ0)}) * (√(2π)/(s^{1/2} Φ''(θ0)^{1/2})) plus controlled remainder terms (e.g., O(s^{-1})), so check even/odd symmetries and parity of factors when simplifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject steepest paths with a local maximum
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple curves through a critical point make F real, select the curve on which Re(F) has a minimum at z0; reject the curve where Re(F) has a maximum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures the integrand decays away from z0 along the chosen path (steepest descent). The text illustrates rejecting Γ2 (where Re(F) has a maximum) and choosing Γ1 (a hyperbolic branch) for F(z) = −i(z^3/3 + z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scaling change-of-variables to match exponent coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose a scaling parameter µ so that after changing variables z → µ z the exponential triad in the integrand simplifies to a standard form e^{−s F(z)} with specified F and s; determine µ by solving coefficient-matching conditions (e.g., A = 2π µ (n − 1/24) and A = π/(12 µ)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting µ appropriately reduces the asymptotic integral to a canonical steepest-descent/Laplace-type integral (here yielding F(z)=i(z−1/z) and s proportional to √(n−1/24)). This scaling identifies the correct large parameter and the critical point location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generating-function singularity principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristic principle: the asymptotic behavior of coefficients F_n of a power series F(w)=∑F_n w^n (with unit disc of convergence) is determined by the location and nature of the singularities of F on the unit circle; the contribution of each singularity corresponds in magnitude to its 'order'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if F is meromorphic in a larger disc with a single pole of order r at w=1, then F_n = P(n) + O(e^{-c n}) for some polynomial P of degree r−1. For more complicated singularities (e.g., essential, branch points, modular-type singularities) interpret and approximate locally to extract contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of modular transformation (Dedekind eta) to approximate generating function near z=0
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit the transformation law η(−1/z) = z^{1/2} η(z) (and the corresponding relation for f) to write f(z) = z^{−1/2} e^{iπ/(12 z)} e^{iπ z/12} f(−1/z); when Im(−1/z) → ∞, f(−1/z) → 1 rapidly, so approximate f by f1(z) = z^{−1/2} e^{iπ/(12 z)} e^{iπ z/12}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This modular-approximation identifies the dominant local behaviour near rationals (in particular z=0) and yields a tractable main-term integral p1(n) plus an error term E(n) involving f(−1/z)−1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing error bounds by choosing contour height δ
rubrics_metrics.description: Two different estimates for f(−1/z)−1 on the contour lead to two types of exponential error contributions in E(n); choose δ to balance these exponents by solving 2π n δ = π/(48 δ) (or the corresponding equality), giving δ proportional to n^{−1/2}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimizing the resulting exponential bound yields the optimal height δ for the contour and controls the error term E(n) to the required size (in the partition example, E(n)=O(e^{K/2 n^{1/2}}) which fits into the overall asymptotic error budget).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replace original contour by steepest-descent contour Γ∗
rubrics_metrics.description: After scaling, identify the critical point and its steepest-descent locus (e.g., for F(z)=i(z−1/z), the unit circle is the curve where F has a minimum at z=i) and replace the integration contour by Γ∗ composed of appropriate segments plus the relevant semicircle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cauchy’s theorem to deform the contour to Γ∗; then split contributions into those from small segments (shown to be negligible) and the principal contribution from the semicircle (evaluated via Laplace/Laplace-type methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate nonprincipal contour contributions as negligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that integrals over segments away from the critical arc are comparatively small (e.g., integrand bounded by a^{3/2} µ^{3/2} = O(1) or exponentially small) and can be absorbed in the error term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the real axis the exponential often has absolute value |z|^{1/2} or otherwise decays, so check explicit bounds to verify these contributions are lower order compared to the main semicircular term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coefficient extraction via contour integral
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent sequence coefficients by p(n) = ∮_γ f(z) e^{−2π i n z} dz with γ a horizontal segment in the upper half-plane (height δ), then analyze which parts of γ contribute most as n→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose γ's height so that f is large near the expected contributing singularity (z=0) and use approximation/modular transformation and steepest descent around that locus to extract asymptotics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of simple connectivity (homotopy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A region Ω is simply connected if any two curves in Ω with the same end-points are homotopic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This topological definition underlies analytic consequences (Cauchy's theorem version) and will be shown equivalent to other formulations (holomorphic simple connectivity, complement connected for bounded regions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holomorphic simple connectivity equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: A region Ω is holomorphically simply connected if whenever γ ⊂ Ω is closed and f is holomorphic in Ω then ∮_γ f(ζ) dζ = 0. Theorem: Ω is holomorphically simply connected if and only if Ω is simply connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction is Cauchy's theorem; the converse uses the Riemann mapping theorem (when Ω ≠ C) to reduce to the unit disc. This provides an analytic characterization useful in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounded-region simple connectivity ↔ complement connected
rubrics_metrics.description: If Ω is a bounded region in C then Ω is simply connected if and only if the complement of Ω is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: for unbounded Ω the statement fails if complement taken in C; if complement is taken in the Riemann sphere the equivalence holds. The proof for one direction uses Runge's theorem to approximate holomorphic functions on compact sets whose complement is connected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Winding number (index) definition and properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed curve γ and z ∉ γ define W_γ(z) = (1/2π i) ∮_γ dζ/(ζ − z). Then W_γ(z) ∈ Z; is constant on each connected component of the complement of γ; and equals 0 on the unbounded component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winding numbers compute how many times γ loops around z and are used to distinguish interior/exterior and to argue about components of complements in proofs of simple connectivity and Jordan's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple connectivity ⇔ no curve in Ω winds around complement points
rubrics_metrics.description: A bounded region Ω is simply connected iff W_γ(z) = 0 for every closed curve γ in Ω and every z ∉ Ω.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The forward direction follows from applying Cauchy's theorem to 1/(ζ−z). For the converse construct a closed curve in Ω quantum-enclosing (via a grid) a bounded complementary component if the complement were disconnected, then find z with nonzero winding, contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan curve theorem for piecewise-smooth curves
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a simple piecewise-smooth closed curve, then its complement consists of two disjoint connected open sets: exactly one bounded simply connected interior Ω and one unbounded exterior U, and the boundary of each is Γ. Moreover W_Γ(z) = 1 for z ∈ Ω and 0 for z ∈ U.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appendix proves this restricted case (piecewise-smooth) and uses construction of parallel curves and grid-based polygonal approximations to identify interior/exterior and establish simple connectivity of the bounded component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct parallel translates γ_ε(t)=γ(t)+ i ε γ'(t) with small ε
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a smooth simple curve Γ0 with arc-length parametrization γ(t), there exists κ1 > 0 such that Γ0 ∩ Γ_ε = ∅ whenever 0 < |ε| < κ1, where Γ_ε is parametrized by γ_ε(t)=γ(t)+ i ε γ'(t).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses uniform continuity of γ' to get local separation bounds and a finite partition of the curve to obtain a global κ1. This device constructs 'parallel' curves used in connectivity/path arguments for the complement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grid approximation to enclose bounded complementary components
rubrics_metrics.description: If a bounded complementary component F1 exists, there is a finite collection of closed grid squares Q_j (from some sufficiently fine uniform grid) such that F1 lies in the interior of the union ∪ Q_j, the union is disjoint from the other complementary component, and the boundary of ∪ Q_j lies in Ω and is a finite union of disjoint simple closed polygonal curves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refine the grid to eliminate 'bad' boundary vertices (where >2 boundary sides meet) and possibly add nearby squares. This polygonal boundary is then used to produce a closed curve in Ω whose winding number about a point in F1 is nonzero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Runge approximation when compact K has connected complement
rubrics_metrics.description: If K is compact and K^c is connected, any function holomorphic on an open set containing K can be uniformly approximated on K by polynomials (Runge's theorem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to approximate f on a compact K containing a contour γ to show ∮_γ f = 0 because polynomial integrals over closed curves vanish; this is used in proving complement-connected ⇒ holomorphically simply connected.
